newsitem.title: IRAN: Iranian newspaper calls for more political debate.
newsitem.headline: Iranian newspaper calls for more political debate.

text.p: A conservative Iranian newspaper on Sunday called for wider political debate at a time when many ordinary Iranians fear a backlash from hardline clerics in forthcoming presidential elections.
"The clerics (religious leaders) are the main guiding force for political activity in our country," said the usually conservative Tehran Times in an editorial.
"However, the complexity of today's affairs requires more coordinated effort, even by the clerics, necessitating the formation of political parties in our society," the paper wrote.
"Political parties are a channel for conveying the views of the masses to the policy makers," it added.
Moderate and conservative factions in Iran, a country of some 60 million and the world's third largest oil exporter, prepare to battle for the presidency in elections slated for May or June.
Iran has dozens of politically active religious, labour and professional associations. They have been authorised after being screened by a government body for their allegiance to Islam.
No formal political parties have been allowed since the Islamic Republic Party, Iran's only party since the 1979 Islamic Revolution, dissolved itself in 1987.
The debate over political parties has been continuing with varying intensity in the past decade with some leading clerics saying such formations would pose a threat to national unity.
President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani, a moderate, is constitutionally barred from running after having served two four-year terms.

The leading candidate, majlis (parliament) speaker Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri, is seen by political analysts as a conservative and close to a more hardline faction often backed by spiritual leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
Many ordinary Iranians fear a win by Nateq-Nouri will see an end to a the relatively liberal political breeze blowing through the 18-year-old Islamic republic.
Young women from Tehran's wealthy northern suburbs now take considerable liberties with the hejab, the covering women must wear in accordance with Islamic law.
Their colourful headscarves are pushed right back to reveal a thick, unIslamic cloud of hair while their short "roupush", a sort of baggy raincoat, does little to cover up designer jeans.
But Nateq-Nouri's leading position in the election contest is sending out conflicting signals to Iranians, many of whom are tired of strict Islamic rules.
"Rafsanjani's the king of the pistachio business, he's a trader," said Abazaari, one of Iran's powerful merchant class, approvingly.
"But what does Nateq-Nouri stand for? No one knows," he said.
